paper_title: OmniXRef: A Unified Framework for Multimodal Multi-Reference Video Editing

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Creative intent in video editing can be expressed through text instructions (e.g., "remove the people"), image references (e.g., subject appearance), video references (e.g., camera movement), or a combination of the above. We introduce OmniXRef, a unified framework for multimodal multi-reference video editing that allows users to combine variable numbers of text, image, and video references to control diverse attributes of a source video. We first devise a unified input design with a reference-bank interface and introduce $R^2$-RoPE to support generalization to more references. Then our model, OmniXRef-Model, uses a single-stream diffusion transformer to jointly process the source video and multimodal context from an MLLM in an interleaved sequence. To address the scarcity of training data for video-reference editing, we construct OmniXRef-Data using synthesis pipelines for different editing tasks and combinations of references. We use curriculum learning to progressively increase task complexity and resolution. To support systematic evaluation of video as a control modality, we introduce OmniXRef-Bench, a benchmark for video-reference attribute transfer across Camera, Motion, Content, Style, and Visual Effects (VFX). Comprehensive evaluations show that our OmniXRef-Model outperforms task-specific baselines and commercial models.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Video editing plays central role in modern digital media creation, enabling applications from film production and advertising to personalized visual storytelling. While traditional video editing often requires time1 consuming manual edits at each step of the editing pipeline, recent advances in generative models have made this more automatic. Given source video, video editing model aims to apply specific edit guided by user intent (e.g., via text prompt) while preserving everything else in the source video. However, describing intricate visual details and how they should dynamically change over time (e.g., camera, lighting, visual effects) can be highly challenging to specify through text and/or image guidance alone, leading to need for video reference. Going further, realizing creative vision may require several multimodal references at once, each contributing different aspect (e.g., object motion, visual effects, camera) of the intended result, as shown in Figure 1. Despite this need, reference-guided video editing has mostly been studied in settings constrained by single reference modality. Existing methods support text instructions with an optional image reference (Cong et al., 2025; Mou et al., 2025; Ju et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026b), multiple image references (Liu et al., 2026b), or single video reference for specific task such as camera control (Luo et al., 2025) and visual effects (VFX) (Jones et al., 2026). Frontier systems increasingly support broader combinations of multimodal references (ByteDance Seed, 2026b; Google DeepMind, 2026; MiniMax, 2026), though many only support references for generation (Kling AI, 2026; Alibaba Cloud Model Studio, 2026; Google Developers, 2025), not editing. In fact, systematic formulation of multimodal multi-reference video editing remains largely underdeveloped. To this end, we introduce OmniXRef, unified framework for multimodal multi-reference video editing. Our omni-reference formulation supports four dimensions: (i) number of references (1, ..., K), (ii) reference modality (text, image, video), (iii) reference attribute (Camera, Motion, Content, Style, VFX) and (iv) composition (text-image, text-video, image-video, text-image-video). The reference inputs are organized through common reference-bank interface, with each bank specifying an editing task and instruction, together with an image or video reference when available, allowing OmniXRef-Model to combine multiple requested edits into one coherent output. OmniXRef-Model integrates an MLLM (Bai et al., 2025b) with single-stream diffusion transformer (DiT), where the MLLM first encodes an interleaved sequence of the system prompt, source video and reference banks to derive the semantic context, then the DiT jointly processes this semantic context, source and reference VAE tokens, and noisy target-video tokens to perform the requested edits while preserving the rest of the source content. To reduce the computational cost of conditioning on multiple video references, we introduce Mix-Patchify (MP), which adapts different patchification granularity for each reference according to its editing task. Furthermore, we introduce R2-RoPE (RoPE with Reserved Reference Slots), which reserves pool of positional slots for reference banks and randomly assigns banks to these slots during training, allowing support for more references at inference than seen in training. We train OmniXRef-Model with curriculum learning, progressively increasing task complexity and resolution to accelerate convergence. Training OmniXRef-Model across reference modalities requires large-scale data covering different reference counts and diverse editing tasks. key challenge is the limited availability of sourcereferencetarget video triplets (Vsrc, Vref , Vtgt) covering wide spectrum of editing tasks. Thus, we develop data synthesis pipelines for single-video-reference editing across five categories: Camera, Motion, Content, Style, and VFX, as well as compositional data synthesis pipeline to support multi-reference editing. These are assembled with text-only and text-image data, resulting in OmniXRef-Data containing 10M training examples. Moreover, to address the absence of comprehensive video-reference editing benchmarks, we introduce OmniXRef-Bench, comprising 125 cases across the five categories. The evaluation protocol measures how faithfully models follow the requested edit and preserve unedited source content, along with the visual quality and temporal consistency of the output. Evaluations on OmniXRef-Bench show that OmniXRef-Model outperforms task-specific baselines in their respective domains and demonstrates better reference adherence and source preservation compared to strong commercial models such as Seedance 2.5 and MiniMax H3. In summary, our contributions are fourfold: We introduce OmniXRef, unified framework that formulates multimodal multi-reference video editing along four dimensions: reference number, modality, attribute, and composition. Our proposed referencebank interface enables flexible combinations of references, with great potential for training at scale. We develop OmniXRef-Model, combining R2-RoPE to support generalization to larger reference sets and Mix-Patchify to reduce the computational cost of conditioning on multiple video references. 2 We construct OmniXRef-Data with data synthesis pipelines for each single-video-reference editing task as well as compositions of two visual references. We introduce OmniXRef-Bench to systematically evaluate reference adherence, visual quality, and source preservation, advancing future work towards video as control modality for editing. Comprehensive evaluations show that our OmniXRef-Model outperforms task-specific baselines and commercial models.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Video Generation and Editing. Video generation is evolving toward comprehensive content-creation systems for multimodal generation and editing (ByteDance Seed, 2026b; Google DeepMind, 2026; Kling Team, 2025; MiniMax, 2026). central research direction is to expand the types of input that users can provide to specify an edit. In this paper, we denote each editing setting by its reference inputs: T, I, and indicate text, image, and video reference, respectively, and V2V denotes source-to-output video editing. EditVerse (Ju et al., 2025), VIVA (Cong et al., 2025), InstructX (Mou et al., 2025), and Kiwi-Edit (Lin et al., 2026b) support TV2V and IV2V. ReBind (Liu et al., 2026b) and TIDE (Liu et al., 2026a) support multiple reference images and associate each with its intended edit. Video references provide temporal information, including camera trajectories, dynamic lighting, and evolving visual effects (VFX), that image(s) cannot demonstrate and text alone may not specify precisely. CamCloneMaster (Luo et al., 2025) and RefVFX (Jones et al., 2026) study camera control and VFX transfer in the VV2V setting, respectively. Recent work (Zhang et al., 2026; Tan et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Qin et al., 2026; Wei et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026) integrates multimodal understanding into video generation and editing through MLLM-based conditioning or joint modeling to handle complex compositions of instructions and references. Building on this progression, OmniXRef provides unified formulation in which each text, image, or video reference is associated with an editing task and instruction, and multiple references can jointly specify the output. Video Editing Datasets and Benchmarks. Training general video editing model requires millions of highquality data. Ditto-1M (Bai et al., 2025a) provides an open-sourced million-scale TV2V dataset. RefVIE (Lin et al., 2026b) and RefVideo-6M (Zi et al., 2026) are highlighted for large-scale IV2V data. Specialized VV2V datasets accompany camera and VFX transfer methods (Luo et al., 2025; Jones et al., 2026). However, large-scale sourcereferencetarget triplets spanning diverse VV2V tasks and their compositions remain scarce. To address this gap, we construct OmniXRef-Data with data synthesis pipelines for each single-video-reference editing task as well as compositions of two visual references. For evaluation, ReCo-Bench (Zhang et al., 2025) and VEFX-Bench (Gao et al., 2026) evaluate TV2V, EditVerseBench (Ju et al., 2025) and RefVIE-Bench (Lin et al., 2026b) cover TV2V and IV2V, and IntelligentVBench (Pan et al., 2026), OmniVideo-1.0 (Kling Team, 2025), and TIDE-Bench (Liu et al., 2026a) extend evaluation to multimodal composition. However, none of them systematically evaluates transferring dynamic attributes from reference videos to source video while preserving the remaining source content. OmniXRef-Bench fills this gap by systematically evaluating reference adherence, visual quality, and source preservation, advancing future work towards video as control modality for editing.

sections.title: 3.2 Mix-Patchify
sections.content: The patchification layer groups the VAE latents of visual input into non-overlapping patches of size = (pt, ph, pw) along the temporal, height, and width axes, and maps each flattened patch to DiT token 4 ej with an MLP specific to p. The pretrained DiT uses = (1, 1, 1) for fine-grained denoising. We retain this granularity for the source and target tokens to preserve detailed source conditioning. Reference tokens, however, do not all require such fine spatial granularity. We therefore introduce Mix-Patchify (MP), which represents each reference at spatial granularity suited to its editing task while keeping pt = 1 throughout to preserve fine-grained temporal resolution for dynamic attributes. More details are provided in Appendix B.2. For patch size p, MP reduces the token count by up to factor of pt ph pw. This substantially lowers training and inference costs (Section 5.7), particularly with multiple references, while maintaining performance and facilitating convergence.

sections.title:
3.3 R2-RoPE
Multimodal multi-reference video editing data become increasingly difficult to construct as the number of
references increases, fundamentally restricting the model’s ability to compose more references at inference.
However, we attribute this limitation partly to a training–inference gap in the default sequential asset indexing
of the 4D RoPE. By default, the 4D RoPE coordinate of token ej is qj = (yj, xj, τj, ρs), where (yj, xj, τj)
denote its height, width, and temporal coordinates, and ρs is the sequential index of the asset to which the
token belongs with regards to the full input sequence. Therefore, during training, the range of ρs is bounded
by the maximum number of assets in a training sequence. In such a case, when the number of references
at inference exceeds those seen during training, the model encounters out-of-distribution RoPE indices and
relative offsets, hindering generalization.
sections.content: To bypass this limitation, we propose R2-RoPE (RoPE with Reserved Reference Slots), which modifies the fourth axis of the default 4D RoPE. Specifically, we reserve fixed slots for the system prompt, the source video, and the noise tokens, together with dedicated pool of slots for reference banks, where the size of this pool is larger than the number of references supported with training data. In practice, we reserve eight slots for reference banks. All tokens belonging to the reference bank Bi share the same fourth-axis coordinate ρi. The key is to randomly sample from the reserved reference slots during training. When training example contains multiple references, non-overlapping slots are selected such that different banks receive distinct coordinates. As this design exposes every reserved reference slot to reference input during training, additional references at inference time remain within the RoPE range seen during training, i.e., becomes in-distribution. R2-RoPE thus avoids the traininginference gap and is able to support more number of references at inference time without requiring training examples for every reference number and combination.

sections.title: 3.4 Curriculum Learning
sections.content: We train OmniXRef-Model in three stages that progressively increase task complexity and output resolution. Stage 1: Single-reference adaptation. We begin at 272P with mixture of TV2V, IV2V, and VV2V examples. This stage adapts the pretrained model to the unified reference-bank interface and establishes task-specific transfer ability while keeping computational cost low. The learning rate starts at 1.5 105 and decays to 1 105 over the first 5,000 steps. Stage 2: Multi-reference composition. At 272P, we retain the Stage 1 tasks and introduce IVV2V and VVV2V examples that combine two visual references. The model learns to use multiple R2-RoPE slots together, providing supervision for compositions beyond any single reference bank. The learning rate remains at 1 105. Stage 3: High-resolution fine-tuning. We increase the resolution of all training examples to 480P while keeping the Stage 2 mixture and other settings unchanged. The stage-wise sampling weights are reported in Table 1.

sections.title: 5.2 Quantitative Comparison
sections.content: Table 2 reports RA, VQ, SP, and the composite Score for each category of OmniXRef-Bench, together with the five-category average of each metric; dashes mark unavailable results. OmniXRef-Model achieves the highest overall Score, RA, and SP, leads on Motion, Content, and Style, and outperforms task-specific baselines in their respective categories and commercial systems overall. The remaining VQ gap relative to commercial systems may reflect differences in pretrained backbone capacity; nevertheless, our model designs deliver strong reference adherence and source preservation while maintaining competitive visual quality. 7 To assess whether our unified formulation generalizes beyond the pretrained DiT used in OmniXRef-Model, we fine-tune MiniMax-H3 on OmniXRef-Data starting from its Ref2VA pretrained checkpoint, without modifying its architecture or adding task-specific components. We refer to the resulting model as OmniXRef (MiniMaxH3). It improves on the original MiniMax-H3 across all five categories and surpasses OmniXRef-Model on Camera and VFX, supporting the portability of our formulation and the practical value of OmniXRef-Data. These results also suggest that more tailored adaptation strategies could yield further gains. Geometry-based camera trajectory errors further support the camera adherence of OmniXRef-Model  (Table 3)  , while results on VEFX-Bench and ReCo-Bench show that it retains competitive TV2V capability (Appendix D).

Although applying (1, 1, 1) patches to all references preserves the most complete reference information, it provides no spatial prior: the model must learn on its own how to extract the requested attribute from long, information-dense reference sequences, which makes learning harder and slows convergence within the same number of training steps. In contrast, Mix-Patchify uses task-specific patch sizes as spatial prior, keeping fine-grained patches where appearance details matter (Content) and coarser patches where the attribute is mainly global or dynamic (Camera, Motion, Style, and VFX), which reduces the learning difficulty, making the model converge faster. R2-RoPE. Replacing R2-RoPE with the default sequential asset indexing causes the smallest overall degradation among the ablations. We attribute this degradation to an intrinsic indexing conflict: under sequential indexing, the fourth-axis index of the noise tokens shifts with the number of references, so for example, the same index denotes the output in samples with one reference but reference in samples with more. Mixing such samples during training therefore introduces conflicting positional signals that make learning harder. Curriculum learning. Without curriculum learning, the model is trained at 480P on the full data pool. Within the same number of training steps, it must acquire all capabilities at once without the inductive bias of easy-to-hard training, which hinders optimization and degrades performance. Training at 480P throughout also makes each step considerably slower. Reference-bank dropout. By default, we drop only the editing instruction edit for classifier-free guidance (Ho and Salimans, 2022), so that the unconditional prediction remains grounded in the same visual reference and the guidance amplifies only the attribute extraction specified by the text instruction. In contrast, dropping the entire bank makes the guidance amplify the influence of the whole reference rather than only the requested attribute, which likely induces reference leakage and degrades performance.

sections.title: 5.6 Analysis of Reference Conditioning
sections.content: Responsiveness to visual references. To verify that OmniXRef-Model actually uses the visual asset in the reference bank rather than relying on the editing instruction alone, we fix the source video and the instruction and only change the reference video. In Figure 4, two references with different sunset lighting are paired with the same instruction, Apply the sunset.... The two outputs reproduce the distinct lighting of their respective visual references, confirming that the visual asset determines the appearance while the instruction specifies which attribute to transfer. Figure 4 Responsiveness to different visual references with fixed source video and edit instruction. Robustness to reference order. With multiple references, natural question is whether the order of the reference banks, that is, which R2-RoPE slot each bank occupies, affects the result. To test this, we keep everything the same while swapping the two reference banks between their slots. As shown in Figure 5, both orders correctly transfer the camera motion and replace the table, indicating that OmniXRef-Model does not collapse into associating particular slots with particular attributes. This robustness stems from randomized slot assignment, which exposes every reserved slot to diverse references during training. As result, although each training sample contains at most two visual references, all reserved slots are activated without bias. Figure 5 Reference-order robustness when swapping reference bank slots in R2-RoPE. Generalization to more references. Figure 6 composes three video references specifying subject motion, camera trajectory, and style, exceeding the maximum of two visual references in any training sample. OmniXRef-Model follows all three references while preserving the source subject and scene thanks to the R2-RoPE design, whereas Seedance 2.5 largely fails to follow the motion and camera references and only partially reproduces the requested style. Figure 6 Compositional generalization to three video references.

sections.title: 5.7 Inference Latency and Computational Cost
sections.content: We measure DiT inference on single NVIDIA A100 GPU, using 480P source and reference videos with 121 frames. We vary both the number of references and the reference patch size in Mix-Patchify (Section 3.2). As Figure 7 shows, more references and finer patches increase both latency and computational cost by lengthening the DiT input sequence. Mix-Patchify reduces both costs, with larger advantage as the number of references grows. Figure 7 Analysis of the inference latency and computational cost.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced OmniXRef, unified framework for multimodal multi-reference video editing, in which text, image, and video references are organized through common reference-bank interface and composed in variable numbers to control distinct attributes of source video. OmniXRef-Model integrates an MLLM with single-stream DiT, employs Mix-Patchify to enable efficient conditioning on multiple video references, and adopts R2-RoPE to generalize beyond the number of references observed during training. To address the scarcity of video-reference editing data and benchmarks, we constructed OmniXRef-Data through synthesis pipelines for Camera, Motion, Content, Style, and VFX, as well as compositions of two references, and established OmniXRef-Bench for the systematic evaluation of reference adherence, visual quality, and source preservation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OmniXRef-Model outperforms both task-specific baselines and commercial systems on OmniXRef-Bench. Further analyses verify that OmniXRef-Model exploits the visual content of each reference, remains robust to the ordering of references, and generalizes to reference compositions beyond the training distribution.

sections.title: A Interleaved Sequence Specification
sections.content: A.1 System Prompt The system prompt Tsys is shared by all reference configurations: You receive source video, then one or more edit banks, each containing task definition, an editing instruction, and optionally its own reference image or video. Apply each bank using only its own reference, take nothing else from any reference, and keep everything the banks do not change as in the source. Output the edited video. A.2 Source and Output Markers Two fixed text markers delimit the roles of the videos in the sequence. The source marker Tsrc, This is the source video to edit:, immediately precedes the source video and identifies it as the video whose unedited content must be preserved. The output marker Tout, The output video is:, immediately precedes the target tokens and signals where the edited video is generated. A.3 Reference Banks Each bank Bi is self-contained edit clause consisting of three parts. Task definition. The task definition task fixes the category of the bank and restricts what may be taken from its reference, while requiring the remaining source content to be preserved. It thereby specifies which attribute to extract, independently of the free-form text instruction. Table 5 lists the task definition of each category verbatim. sections.title: C Benchmark Evaluation Protocol
sections.content: C.1 Category-Specific Evaluation OmniXRef-Bench evaluates single-video-reference editing across Camera, Motion, Content, Style, and VFX. Video-reference editing raises three separate questions: whether the output adopts the requested dynamic attribute from the reference, whether the result looks and moves convincingly, and whether everything else from the source remains intact. model could produce an attractive video while ignoring the requested edit, or copy the desired attribute along with unrelated reference content; neither is successful edit. We use Gemini 3.8 Flash (Google, 2026) as VLM judge for three separate criteria: Reference Adherence (RA) assesses the requested reference attribute, Visual Quality (VQ) assesses the output quality, and Source Preservation 16 (SP) assesses source information that should remain unchanged, including unwanted reference-content transfer. The judge returns structured labels that we convert into scores deterministically; the complete category-specific prompts are listed in Appendix F. C.2 Deterministic Scoring The judge outputs only closed-set labels, which deterministic rules convert into scores on 05 scale  (Table 6)  . Each criterion first receives base score by averaging the scores of its labels; category-specific caps then penalize failures that the average alone would miss. Leakage is graded by the number of source attributes that the SP judge labels as imported from the reference: two or more clear imports are major, one clear import is minor, and only possible imports are suspected. The composite Score is Score = 0.45 RA + 0.25 min(VQ, RA) + 0.30 SP, (6) where bounding VQ by RA prevents visually appealing outputs that ignore the requested edit from scoring well, and the leakage caps prevent high scores on other criteria from compensating for severe unwanted changes. All caps are applied per example before averaging; consequently, the reported mean RA, VQ, and SP do not in general determine the mean Score, and we report VQ before the min(, RA) bound so that visual quality can be distinguished from editing success. sections.title: E Limitations
sections.content: OmniXRef-Model supports attribute-level control but cannot yet reliably disentangle finer-grained factors within an attribute. For example, the model may transfer facial expressions and body poses together from motion reference, making it difficult to apply either independently (Figure 8). Scaling to larger reference compositions is also constrained by the difficulty of constructing high-quality training data in which the target video incorporates all requested edits. Although our reserved-slot design supports generalization beyond the reference counts seen during training, performance degrades substantially with four or more references. Our training data also underrepresent content beyond natural scenes, particularly VFX involving text rendering, indicating need for greater diversity in visual content and editing operations. Finally, training is currently limited to resolutions up to 480P, and the effectiveness of our framework for higherresolution editing at 720P or 4K remains unexplored. Figure 8 Coupled transfer of facial expression and body pose from Motion reference.

sections.title: F VLM Judge Prompts
sections.content: This section lists the complete prompts that Gemini 3.8 Flash (Google, 2026) receives when scoring OmniXRefBench.
